paragraphs: Here's what I take from this one, friend. Esther had a perfectly good reason to sit tight. She knew the law about going to the king uninvited, and she told Mordecai she hadn't been summoned in thirty days (Esther 4:11). Staying quiet in that palace looked like the safe move, and Mordecai wasn't having it.

Mordecai says, "Do not imagine that because you are in the king's palace you alone will escape the fate of all the Jews." (Esther 4:13) Then he asks, "And who knows if perhaps you have come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14) He doesn't say it as a fact. He asks it as a question, and I think that's why it hits so hard. Comfort can fool you into thinking a hard moment belongs to somebody else, and a moment that finds you may be a moment you're standing in on purpose.

Now look at what Esther does with that question. She doesn't charge in alone. She asks the people to fast for her, and she and her maidens fast too (Esther 4:16). Then comes the line: "And if I perish, I perish!" (Esther 4:16) Courage like that doesn't come from feeling fearless, friend. It comes from deciding that doing the right thing matters more than staying comfortable, and from not walking into it alone. So when your moment shows up, ask for help, get ready, and take the step.
